claims.claim: at Gardner Lake, Connecticut, ice push built a ridge 0.6–1.2 m high (Pessl 1969, known from a search summary)
claims.quote: is parallel to the shoreline, and is 0.6- 1.2 m high
claims.conditions: the best-developed ridge, on the lake's northwest shore. The ridges postdate a dam built in the early 1880s, so the ridge is about 80 years of push (p. 1). It is made of reworked glaciofluvial beach deposits, with boulders up to 0.6 m. In the 1966–67 winter studied, push itself built only small ridges 15.2–25.4 cm high and a discontinuous ridge of ~14 m³ along 260 m of shore; ~90 % of that was washed away by waves before the next winter (p. 12)
claims.note: Now read in full: drop 'known from a search summary'. Gardner Lake is about 2.8 km long and 0.8 km wide (p. 1). The paper's next clause says lakes under ~0.8 km across 'may be too small for appreciable push' (Wagner 1970), yet this ~0.8-km-wide lake has well-developed ridges.

claims.claim: at Gardner Lake an ice-push ridge formed 0.6–1.2 m high and 1.2–3.1 m wide (Pessl 1969, as restated by Gatto, Ferrick & Calkins 2001)
claims.quote: It is 1.2-3.1 m wide and asymmetric in transverse profile
claims.conditions: as above: the ridge accumulated since the 1880s dam; its back (landward) slope is commonly steeper than its front (lakeward) slope; perennial vegetation grows on it
claims.note: Cite Pessl directly. 'Formed' should not suggest a single winter: the 1966–67 season added only a small, mostly ephemeral deposit.

claims.claim: the thrust at Gardner Lake came mainly from thermal expansion, not wind (Pessl 1969; relayed by a search summary)
claims.quote: strongly support the hypothesis of thermal expansion as the principal cause of ice thrusting
claims.conditions: one winter of observation (9 February–11 March 1967). The ice was frozen to the whole shore and no leads opened even in a northwest gale over 48.3 km/h on 1 March. Breakup winds kept ice off the northwest shore. The author allows that wind-driven floating ice may have contributed in other years

notes: Other values: the average net shoreward movement of the surveyed ice was 1.0 m over the 30-day period (nine stakes 0.9–1.2 m). An ice-temperature rise of about 1 °C/h for 5–11 h (6 h in the conclusions) was enough to drive ice against the shore; air temperature was a poor guide to ice temperature above −5 °C. The author's general statement: thermal expansion 'is probably limited to relatively small bodies of water or to confined parts of larger bodies' (p. 1), and wind push matters on coasts and large lakes. A push deposit survives only where it lies beyond the reach of waves and above the normal swings of lake level (p. 12). That bears on the paper's inference about a lag at the winter waterline.
